task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-11-02, in the area of lineup and matchup effects):
Changing the offensive five itself moves shot mix, showing the design can detect personnel effects.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

methodological_questions: How to isolate the effect of replacing the entire offensive five on shot mix while controlling for opponent defense and game context?
What is the minimum detectable shift in shot mix given the number of full-five offensive substitutions?
Can the design distinguish a true personnel-driven shift from regression to the mean or game-situation confounding?
How should shot mix be measured (per-play-type shares vs. a multivariate distance)?

historical_evidence.finding: Offenses attack the rim more when the opponent has no big on the floor: DRIVE +0.82pp, 3PA -1.79pp, rim share not significant, PPP +0.008 (SE 0.007) t=+1.1; verdict WEAK/SMALL.
Rank-1 openers CUT-centered and INFEASIBLE; CUT target 14-18% exceeds stretch ceiling of 2-6% for every team.
Flat non-decaying play-type lifts collapse under within-team baseline; team-quality confound invalidates PIS gate.
DRIVE and PNR lag-1 PPP effects disappear after controlling for game state (score, period, clock) and within-team baseline.

failed_approaches.what_failed: opponent lineup adaptation study to produce conclusive paper
failed_approaches.why: effect sizes small (rim share +0.123 SE 0.295); PPP t=+1.1 not significant; verdict weak/small
C_artifact: CUT target 3-10x stretch ceiling; infeasible recommendations produced
flat non-decaying lifts disappear under within-team baseline; team-quality confound

failed_approaches.what_failed: sequence-memory lag effects with game-state controls
failed_approaches.why: DRIVE and PNR lag-1 effects vanish when adding controls / within-team baseline; artifact

evidence_establishes: Even a large defensive personnel change (opponent losing its rim big) produces only modest, sometimes non-significant shot mix shifts.
Play-type share analyses are vulnerable to confounding by team quality and game state, requiring within-team comparisons and careful controls.
Certain play types (e.g., CUT) have hard capacity ceilings that limit how much shot mix can change, and feasibility must be considered.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether changing the offensive five itself produces a detectable shot mix shift.
The magnitude or power of a design-detection test using full five-man offensive substitutions.
How to completely isolate offensive personnel changes from simultaneous opponent lineup changes.
own_inferences: A design-detection test is plausible as a within-game, within-team comparison of shot mix before and after complete five-man substitutions, controlling for opponent defense and game state.

The primary threat is confounding because offensive substitutions often coincide with defensive substitutions; restricting to possessions where only the offense changes may severely limit sample size.
A composite measure of shot mix (e.g., cosine distance) can aggregate across play types and improve power over testing each play type individually.
The effect size likely varies by team and specific entering/leaving players, but the goal is to show any detectable shift, establishing sensitivity.
uncertainties: The actual frequency of full-five offensive substitutions per game and the number of possessions where the opponent five remains unchanged is unknown without a data pull.
The minimum detectable effect size may be larger than the true shift if only a fraction of possessions are usable.
Reliability of the rule-based play-type classifier across different lineups could introduce differential measurement error.

historical_effect.explanation: Historical evidence ([prior work], SF-[prior work]) reveals that even large lineup alterations produce modest shot mix changes and that confounding from team quality/game state easily masks effects. This elevates the required rigor for controls and power analysis, shifting the design from a simple comparison to one with strict conditioning on opponent and game context.

blocking_constraints.text: Full-five offensive substitutions may be infrequent; not yet measured whether the possessional sample size is sufficient.
Opponent defensive changes often co-occur; isolating the offensive five effect demands either coincident unchanged defense or comprehensive controls.

prior_work.summary: No prior study tested the effect of changing the entire offensive five on shot mix. The closest work examined opponent absence ([prior work]) and play-type memory artifacts, highlighting small effects and confounding.

risks.text: Opponent defensive lineup may change simultaneously with the offensive five, biasing the estimated personnel effect.
Full-five changes occur only a limited number of times per game; the resulting possessions may be insufficient to detect moderate shot mix shifts per play type.
Testing several play types or a composite measure plus sub-tests requires multiplicity adjustment.
Low-frequency play types (e.g., CUT, PUTBACK) have floor effects that can dampen measurable changes.
If pre-substitution shot mix is assessed over a short window, regression to the mean could masquerade as a substitution effect.
Play-type classification error may vary with player identity, potentially confounding comparisons across lineups.

design.estimand: Causal effect of replacing the entire on-court offensive unit (all five players) on the team's play-type share distribution, controlling for opponent defensive lineup and game context.
design.unit: Stint-level play-type proportions (possessions grouped by a contiguous interval with the same ten players on the floor).
design.sample: NBA 2022-23, 2023-24, 2024-25 regular seasons and playoffs. Exclude garbage time (last 4 minutes, margin > 20). Identify all stints and mark transitions where the offensive team substitutes all five players. Retain only those transitions where the defensive five remained unchanged across the substitution; alternatively, control for opponent lineup via fixed effects if enough overlap exists.
design.power: Pilot estimate: [prior work] detected a -1.79pp 3PA shift with SE 0.31 from ~1M possessions. Assume full-five transitions yield ~90k total possessions across 3 seasons (roughly 100 transitions per team-season, 10 possessions each). A similar effect size would remain detectable. A composite shot-mix distance (e.g., cosine distance) will be used as the primary endpoint to aggregate signal across play types and improve power.
design.controls: Fixed effects for team, opponent defensive lineup (or opponent team), period, score margin at stint start, and possession start type (e.g., off defensive rebound, dead ball). Sensitivity analysis using continuous covariates for margin and clock.
design.falsification: Placebo test: compare shot mix before vs. after pseudo-transitions where the offense did not change (timeouts, quarter breaks) but a 'fake' split is imposed; any significant effect would invalidate the design. Also permute the timing of substitutions within games to verify that no systematic confound exists.
design.multiplicity: Use a single primary test on the composite distance measure (permutation-based p-value). Secondary per-play-type tests will be reported after Bonferroni correction.
design.decision_rule: Reject the null of no shot mix change if the permutation test on cosine distance yields p < 0.01 and at least one major play type (e.g., SPOT_UP, DRIVE, PNR) shows a consistent direction across teams not attributable to a single outlier.
design.data_version: NBA stats API per-game files as of 2026-11-02; play-type labels from the project's production classifier v2.1.
